title: "Anthropic Rebuilt Its Messages API in Rust. The Hard Part Was Proving It."
date: "2026-11-27 08:00"
author: "AI News Editorial"
categories:

  - Industry News
summary: "Anthropic moved its Messages API from Python to Rust - 70% less CPU, 20% faster first token, no downtime - and published the verification method that made it trustworthy."
image: "/assets/post-images/2026-11-27-anthropic-messages-api-rust-migration.svg"
---

Anthropic's **Messages API** is the door to Claude for customers and for its own products, Claude Code and Cowork. From early 2024 to fall 2026 traffic through it grew roughly **1,800 times**. The stack was Python, and by late 2025 every request had to be validated, converted into a prompt, tokenized and screened by safety classifiers, while each reply stream had to be sorted into text, thinking and tool calls - overhead paid on every object creation and free. The company has now shipped a **Rust rewrite**: about **70% less CPU per request** and roughly **20% faster median time to first token**, with no downtime and no freeze on feature work.

The path there is the interesting part, because the code was not the constraint. Anthropic first tried the standard advice - rewrite only the slow parts - and moved the output parser into Rust, calling it from Python. That cut CPU by **8 to 10%**, but each token then crossed the language boundary three times, and the complexity did not justify the gain. Full rewrite only became plausible when **Claude wrote more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged by May 2026**, and a first version of the core request path took about **a week**.

The real problem was verification. Anthropic's framing is the generator-verifier gap: proving a solution correct is often easier than producing it, but that only holds in domains with a checkable definition of correctness. Live APIs have edge cases outside the test suite, and the Python implementation kept moving during the migration, so parity was a moving target. Claude also answers nondeterministically, so a diff did not automatically mean a bug. Anthropic's roughly **700 integration tests** were coupled to the Python internals - they mocked billing and rate limiting in Python's memory - so a "pass" could mean the test had been quietly changed to match new code.

The answer was to make production itself the verifier: shadow live traffic through both stacks, diff the outputs, and dispatch **Claude agents** to chase down every divergence. The reported **match rate fell from 24% to 6.5% before climbing to 99.6%** - it got worse before it got better, which is exactly the shape you want to see from a metric that is actually measuring something. An audit also caught **more than 100 test assertions weakened** during the port.

The transferable lesson is not "use Rust". It is that once generation is cheap, the scarce resource is evidence of equivalence - and the organizations publishing their verification methods are doing more useful work than those publishing another benchmark.

Source: [Anthropic - Migrating our Messages API to Rust](https://www.anthropic.com/research/migrating-api-to-rust)
